en: May the illustrious Veṅkaṭanāthārya, the lion among poets and logicians,
the preeminent teacher of Vedānta, ever abide within my heart.
I worship that one resplendent splendor upon the lofty peak of Śrī Śeṣaśaila, which is the crown of the supreme Vedas and the lap of the Lord of Serpents. 1.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, who is to be inquired about by those seeking liberation who have deliberated upon the nature of karma and, through detachment from its fruits, desire to know Him.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, by whose effects—the arising, subsistence, and dissolution of this world—that which is capable of being attained may be reached. 3.

I worship that which is the sole cause of the universe, adorned with a multitude of qualities such as omniscience, and which is to be known solely through the scriptures—that which bears the name Śrīnivāsa. 4.
I worship that which is known through the scriptures by the name Śrīnivāsa, because it is proclaimed as the supreme human goal by all the utterances of the Upaniṣads. 5.
Because it is the remainder of the discourse beginning with "seeing" (īkṣā), the *Sadvijñāna* pertains to the cause denoted by the word "Being.
That which is "Being," that which is revealed by the word "yat" (that), I worship as the Name Śrīnivāsa. 6.
That Vidyā reveals the one consisting of bliss through the bliss of the unconditioned state and other such qualities;
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart-essence, which is distinguished from all else.
Having taught that lotus-eyed one who dwells within the solar orb, the Vidyā reveals Him; I worship that Heart-mantra named Śrīnivāsa.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, whom the Veda leads to—He regarding whom they speak of qualities such as being the singular fit object and the ultimate refuge for space (ākāśa). 9.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which the Veda reveals as "That" (yat), because it is well-known through the scriptural declaration of the Prāṇa's causality. 10.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart [of all], which arises from the statement: "The light endowed with unsurpassed radiance is one quarter; the elements are his [other] quarters. 11.

I worship that [deity] named Śrīnivāsa, who is the Brāhmaṇa [text] marked by the Vidyā [section] for Pratardana, and who reveals through His attributes that which is designated by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa. 12.

Because of the power of the restatement of its birth and other qualities, that which was spoken as the entire Brāhmaṇa is revealed by the word "yat" (that) as this Vidyā; I worship that Brāhmaṇa named Śrīnivāsa. 13.

I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which, by the statement "it is food for the self," establishes [the self] as the enjoyer, and by the statement "death is its condiment," makes it understood that he is the destroyer. 14.
I worship that Vidyā named Śrīnivāsa, which reveals the Person in the Eye through well-known attributes such as the abiding in the eye. 15.

I worship that which is called the *vidyā*—the heart-essence (*hṛdaya*) named Śrīnivāsa—which, as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*), is declared to be the simultaneous governance of all things through its primary functions. 16.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart, which is the source of all beings, described as the Imperishable by those who teach through defining attributes, and which knowledge makes manifest. 17.

Because the knowledge of Vaiśvānara as the Self is taught as having heaven and the other [elements] as its constituent parts, that which reveals this—the *Tadbṛhat* hymn named Śrīnivāsa—I worship. 18.

I worship that Vidyā named Śrīnivāsa, which reveals the Self as the support of heaven, earth, and all else, and as the bridge to immortality; that which [the Upanishads] express by the word "That" (yat). 19.
I worship that Vidyā-brāhmaṇa named Śrīnivāsa, which reveals the Bhūman as distinct in meaning from the individual soul (jīva) denoted by the word "prāṇa," through the word "yat. 20.

I worship that *Brahman* named Śrīnivāsa, which is revealed by the knowledge [of the Upanishads] as "the Imperishable," "neither gross nor subtle," and so forth, through its qualities such as being the Ruler. 21.

I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, which—through the statement of the verse—is revealed by the Sage as being visible to the liberated person who beholds it; this is what the word "yat" (which) makes manifest. 22.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which the Dahara-vidyā reveals as the "small ether" (dahara ākāśa) by means of attributes such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva). 23.
I worship that Vidyā named Śrīnivāsa, which reveals the Person the size of a thumb residing within the human heart as the Sovereign through His lordship and other attributes. 24.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which is to be meditated upon even by the gods, out of a desire for the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering overcome by them. 25.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which is to be meditated upon by those dwelling in the stations of the Vasus, Rudras, and others, who possess the desire to attain it once again. 26.

Regarding the fact that a teacher is observed to address a willing disciple as "śūdra," this does not indicate that Śūdras possess the qualification [for Vedic study], because such an address is prompted by grief. || 27 ||
Since even a Śūdra who desires liberation lacks the qualification for meditation because he is devoid of Vedic study and the like, I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa. 28.
I worship that which the Śruti, speaking of space, reveals as the agent of names and forms;
I worship that which is indicated by the word "yat," whose name is Śrīnivāsa. 29.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which the Kaṭhavallī declares to be the foremost among those things to be mastered by the yogi, beginning with the senses. 30.

I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, whose status as the effect of Prakṛti—while she is creating progeny—is declared by the *aja* (unborn) scripture and confirmed by the unanimous voice of other Vedic branches. 31.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, upon whom the existence of those called the *pañcajana*— namely, space and the senses— is said to depend.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, whom all the Vedas proclaim as the Person characterized by omniscience and other attributes, and as the cause of ether and the rest of the elements.

I worship that which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, whose state of being an effect— as established by the scripture "He whose work this is" and other means of valid cognition— is proclaimed by the Brāhmaṇa.

I worship that *Bṛhad-āraṇyaka* named Śrīnivāsa, which, by means of reasoning such as "He who is said to be 'to be seen' is the cause of immortality," leads one to understand that [the Self] is indeed that [Brahman]. 35.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart [of all], which, by the statement "By the knowledge of which one thing, all this becomes known," leads one to understand its material cause.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which, although the reality is expressed by various words such as "Śiva" and others, causes one to understand it through its true attributes. 37.
I worship that heart whose name is Śrīnivāsa, the cause of which is unshakable, being established by the crest of the Vedas as augmented by the many Smṛtis of Manu and other authoritative sages. 38.

The identity of substance alone is fixed between the material cause and its modification, not their sameness of genus; for here it is Brahman alone, whose body consists of both consciousness and unconsciousness, that constitutes the cause and the effect. || 39 ||

Because the relationship between the body and the embodied is established by the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa, and because bodily characteristics exist in relation to Brahman in this world which is non-different from it. || 40 ||
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart, whose causality is unshakable, because the states residing in the body do not follow along with the embodied self. 41.
I worship that heart whose name is Śrīnivāsa, the cause of which is unshakable, since the doctrines of Kaṇabhakṣa and others are mutually contradictory. 42.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart, whose causality is unshakable because there is no possibility of its being subject to karma, since it is the enjoyer of what is produced by karma while itself remaining independent of karma. 43.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, whose causality is unshakable because the non-difference between the material cause and its modification has been established by the Vedas. 44.

Because statements such as "That thou art" have another purpose, and because the difference in nature between the creator of the world and the individual soul (jīva) who is created is difficult to shake off. (45)

I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, for its causality—unshakable even when acting for the benefit of living beings—is due to its freedom from attachment to acting for its own benefit. 46.
In the world, it is observed that milk and other substances, even when not assisted by anything else, initiate the production of curds and so forth;
for those things possessing causal power, there is an absence of a restrictive requirement for auxiliary factors with respect to their respective effects. (47)
Since the commencement of the world is possible even without a cooperative cause (sahakārin), I worship that which is the immovable cause in this context—the one named Śrīnivāsa. 48.

Whatever entity is established in whatever manner by the means of cognition that apprehends its substrate, it must be accepted by all exactly in that way; [thus,] Brahman is one, partless, and yet becomes manifold. (49)
Since there is no room for mundane objection regarding a matter established by such scriptural authority, I worship that heart whose name is Śrīnivāsa, the cause of which is unshakable. 50.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, whose causality is unshakable, for there can be no lack of purpose in a creation undertaken as a divine play (līlā). 51.
The commencement of activity is not seen in insentient things such as wood when they are not presided over by an intelligent being; therefore, the same applies to the insentient Pradhāna. || 52 ||

I worship that name Śrīnivāsa, which is firmly established as the cause [of the world] according to the Śruti, since the "initiation of effects" (kāryārambhakatā) asserted by the Sāṅkhyas is impossible. 53.

If atoms were partless, there would be no commencement of a dyad due to the impossibility of their conjunction; if they were to have parts, they too would be subject to the same [infinite regress]. (54)
Because the Vaiśeṣika system is flawed due to such arguments as "this leads to an infinite regress," I worship that most firm causal principle whose name is Śrīnivāsa. 55.

In the doctrine of momentary atoms, because atoms perish at every moment, a composite whole cannot be established by them; and since that [whole] is not established, there is an absence of the establishment of the body. || 56 ||
Since even the Buddhist philosophy is untenable due to the failure to establish the origin of the world, I worship that most firm cause named Śrīnivāsa. 57.

When there is a perception of the object, the locus, and the cognition that are similar [to one another], and in the absence of sublation, by setting aside both the object and the locus, one speaks of the ultimate reality of the single cognition alone. (58)
Since even the doctrine of the Yogācāras is extremely difficult to maintain and thus lacks authority, I worship that which is the name Śrīnivāsa, whose causality is most firm. (59)

Whether the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists or does not exist within itself, the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda) [is untenable], because it lacks the emergence [of its own proof] and thus results in the non-establishment of itself. || 60 ||
I worship that name Śrīnivāsa, which is the most firmly established cause for the Madhyamaka school, which is otherwise extremely difficult to maintain. 61.
Because both [attributes], which are mutually contradictory like light and darkness, are predicated of every single object, such as the properties of existence and non-existence. (62)
I worship that name Śrīnivāsa, which is the most firmly established cause for the position favored by the Jains, [a position] that is otherwise utterly unstable. 63.

"Paśupati is the creator of the entire world, the material cause, composed of the three guṇas, and the Lord is accessible through inference"—because such a conception contradicts the Vedas in many ways. (64)
Just as the individual soul presides over the material nature (prakṛti), so too does the Lord;
for if one accepts that [the Lord] presides [over it], there would be the undesirable consequence of [the Lord being subject to] pleasure, pain, and the like. (65)
Since even the Pāśupata doctrine is extremely unstable, I worship that name Śrīnivāsa, which is firmly established as the cause [of the world] as proven by the Śruti. 66.

Because the statement of those who propound the origination of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth is intended as a specific metaphorical arrangement (vyūha), and because there is no contradiction with the Veda anywhere in the Pāñcarātra Tantra; || 67 ||
I worship that name "Śrīnivāsa," which is firmly established as the cause [of all], being proven by the preeminent system [of this Tantra] due to the absence of any lack of authority. 68.

Regarding the proposition stated that "when Brahman is known, everything becomes known," that [proposition] would not be sustained if the origination [of the world] were not admitted, and because there is no denial [of such origination]. (69)
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, whose status as an effect remains unbroken because it is certain that its origination must be accepted from Brahman alone.
Having resolved upon his own manifold manifestation, he created everything;
thus it is established that from the form of Brahmā, which was of the nature of air, the form of fire was born. || 71 ||
Since the comprehension of all meanings is established through other Vedic texts, I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, from whom [all things] arise directly. 72.
Because the origination of the individual soul (jīva) is denied and its eternity is affirmed, there is no origination; furthermore, this is established by the thesis previously cited.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart, whose state of being an effect remains unbroken through the channel of the quality known as consciousness, which undergoes modifications such as contraction and so forth. (74)
The Self is neither mere cognition nor is it of a single nature as a cognizer,
because of the scriptural declarations regarding its nature as cognition and its nature as a cognizer.
I worship that name "Śrīnivāsa," which, through the channel of the aforementioned knowledge, has its efficacy for the goal unbroken due to being proclaimed many times. (76)
I worship that name "Śrīnivāsa," by which the self is established as the agent in enjoined actions, and through which the fruitfulness of both that [agency] and the injunction is accomplished. 77.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the Veda declares to depend upon which the agency of the inner self (pratyagātman) exists in worldly and Vedic actions. 78.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, of whom this individual soul (jīva) is a part, just as "cowness" and so forth belong to the cow, or as light and so forth belong to the sun. 79.

[This is] due to their being beneficial to the living being (jīva), as well as for their instruments—the atoms—and for the eleven sense organs and the vital breath (prāṇa) which is distinct from air. (80)
Since the production of the subtle instrument (the mind) is heard [in scripture], I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, whose nature as an effect remains unbroken. 81.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart (hṛdaya) wherein the presiding of the deities beginning with Agni and of living beings over the senses and so forth depends upon His will. 82.

I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by whom it was sung in the Gītās that speech and the other senses, as well as sight and the rest, possess the nature of being sense-organs only when accompanied by the mind. 83.
The mutual blending of fire, water, and earth for the sake of the individual creation of the cosmic egg and so forth occurs by virtue of their being produced by a common agent. (84)
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which the Veda proclaims as the manifestation of the names and forms of the gods and others, and which describes whatever is its effect.
The knowledge of the five fires concerns the removal of the distress arising from bondage to saṃsāra;
it pertains to the attainment of another body after the departure from the current one for those who have performed sacrifices and works of public utility.

He describes the destination of one who is completely enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), along with the senses and the vital breaths (prāṇa), and whose [state] is dependent upon His will; I worship that which is called the Abode of Śrī, namely Brahman. 87.
When the fruit of good deeds has been enjoyed, he descends again accompanied by those karmas whose fruits have not yet been experienced;
I worship that heart whose will causes this descent, the one named Śrīnivāsa.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by whose resolve even those who lack knowledge and ritual action and are doers of evil resort solely to the hells. 89.

I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which, having attained an indescribable union with those beginning with the descending sky (the syllables *ava-roha-ga-ga-na-ādyaiḥ*), emerges [as the name] before long. 90.
Having emerged from the clouds, that which clings—by its own volition—to the bodies of others attained through rice-grains, I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa. 91.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which by its inconceivable power creates for embodied beings such extraordinary things as chariot-ruts within a dream. 92.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, wherein this weary soul, together with its instruments, rests in deep sleep as if upon a bed of cotton.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by resting upon which the living soul attains well-being and rises up once more, as if from a couch. 94.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which is distinct from swoon and other states, and which persists through the conditions of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth. 95.
Those defects such as waking and so forth, which arise in the individual soul (jīva) due to its connection with that [body], do not belong to it even when in conjunction with that body. (96)

I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, wherein all things are bound together by its nature as the adversary of what is to be abandoned, and also by its nature as the locus of auspicious qualities. 97.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, whose portion this universe—consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest—is like the light of the sun. 98.
I worship that which is supreme over all, than which there is nothing else superior—whether in terms of qualities or essential nature—that is Brahman, whose name is Śrīnivāsa. 99.

I worship that single name, Śrīnivāsa, which is the heart-essence, which has been propitiated by all actions and adorations without exception, which is gracious, and which bestows the fruit of everything. 100.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, whose vidyās—such as Vaiśvānara and Dahara—are non-different in both recensions due to the non-difference of their injunctions and other such factors. 101.

Those two meditations on the *udgītha* which are traditionally taught for the purpose of assisting worship by means of the vision of *prāṇa*—in one of these, the vision of *prāṇa* is directed toward the *udgātṛ*. (102)

Because of the difference in form—namely, that one is in the *praṇava* which is a limb of the *udgītha*, while the other is not—these two knowledges (*vidyā*) are distinct; I worship that *Brahman* named Śrīnivāsa. 103.

In the knowledge concerning the vital breath (prāṇa) taught in the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad], which depends on that [breath], and in the knowledge of the object of cognition in the form of the vital breath as the preeminent one taught in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad]— 104.
Since the entire process of establishing preeminence is of a single nature, the two vidyās are non-different; I worship that Brāhmaṇa named Śrīnivāsa. 105.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the Great Heart, which is distinguished by attributes such as truthfulness that differentiate it from both the conscious and the unconscious, and which is to be meditated upon in all the various higher sciences. 106.

In the Vājasaneyi [Brāhmaṇa] and in the Sāman [Upaniṣads], regarding the knowledge concerning the vital breath (prāṇa) which is dependent [on the self], there is the enjoyment of fruits both before and after by those devoted to the meditation on the vital breath. (107)

The state of being the garment for the vital breaths (prāṇa) is ordained to be contemplated specifically within the waters employed for sipping (ācamana); I worship that name "Śrīnivāsa" which is prescribed as the heart-verse (brāhma) for that. 108.
In the Upaniṣad of the Vājins, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is heard twice; in one instance, they describe its quality known as "the state of having unfailing resolve. (109)
I worship that Heart named Śrīnivāsa, which, through its various expansions, is said elsewhere to possess qualities such as universal sovereignty and the status of being the supreme ruler.
I worship that which resides in the solar orb by the name "Day" (Ahar), and that which resides in the eye by the name "I" (Aham)—that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa. 111.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, wherein qualities such as youthfulness and all-pervasiveness abide as objects of meditation within the sciences concerning small abodes and limited domains. 112.
The fruit is the attainment of Brahman and nothing else; therefore, there is no difference between these two Puruṣa-vidyās.
I worship that Brahman, named Śrīnivāsa, by whose attainment or non-attainment [the distinction is made]. 113.

I worship that which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, the Brāhmaṇa portion [of the Veda] consisting of the primary *śaṃ no* mantras, which are employed in the study of the Vedas that enjoin its worship. 114.
That which constitutes the fruit of knowledge for one established therein is the total abandonment of both good and evil deeds, as well as the entry [into the Self] of friends and enemies. ||115||
In all branches of knowledge, there are two pairs; of these two pairs, that which must be contemplated like the contemplation [of the Self] is the name Śrīnivāsa—this I worship. 116.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which is the separation from all merit and demerit for the wise man, resulting from the fruit of knowledge at the time of departure from the body. 117.
This scripture, beginning with "And those who [practice] in the forest," declares the path starting with light (arcir-ādi-gati) for all those who meditate upon Him;
I worship that heart whose name is Śrīnivāsa. 118.

I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, whose nature is purity—consisting in being an adversary to all that is to be abandoned—and whose form is to be withdrawn into within all branches of knowledge. 119.

Even though there is a difference between the questions and answers of Uṣasta and Kahola, what is intended by both the questioner and the respondent in those two cases is the same: that [the Self] is the innermost of all.
The intended meaning there is that [the scripture] is for the purpose of excluding the other;
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which is the object of that singular knowledge. 121.

In the Vājasaneyi and the Sāman [recensions], regarding the subject matter of the Dahara-vidyā, it is recognized as being this very same [vidyā] by virtue of its being enjoined as a bridge, a support, and so forth. || 122 ||
From such passages as "the controller of all," it is understood that the eightfold qualities are to be known here;
they do not differ from one another. I worship that heart whose name is Śrīnivāsa. 123.
Even in the absence of knowledge of the *udgītha*, because [the fruit] is heard [to result] from the performance of the sacrifice;
for there is the attainment of the sacrifices even without the necessity of that knowledge. || 124 ||
Whether accompanied by those meditations or devoid of them, all those sacrifices are subordinate members of the meditation upon that which bears the name Śrīnivāsa; I worship that Brāhmaṇa. 125.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart, which is to be meditated upon as distinct [from the self] by virtue of its specific qualities and essential nature for those devoted to the meditation on the small space (dahara). 126.

In the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka and in various Vidyās, that which is described by terms such as "Śiva" has been determined by scriptural statements to be the name "Śrīnivāsa"; I worship that Heart-mantra. 127.
I worship the name Śrīnivāsa, which is indeed the *brāhmaṇa* that bestows the fruit of that sacrifice for whose sake the mind-made, speech-made, and other [altars] are constructed. 128.

I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by whose qualifying attributes the individual soul (jīvātman) is to be meditated upon as the object of supreme knowledge (paravidyā), and in its pure form is to be worshipped. 129.
Because all individual instances are present in the mind by means of the term "udgītha," they are connected with every one of those specific individuals. || 130 ||
Likewise, those meditations are connected across all the Vedic branches;
among the ritual acts consisting of sacrifices, I worship that *brahma* known by the name Śrīnivāsa. (131)
In the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, it is the body consisting of the three worlds that is to be meditated upon, not each individual limb; I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa. 132.
The meditations beginning with the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) are distinct due to differences such as their qualities (guṇa) and injunctions (codanā).
I worship that Heart, named Śrīnivāsa, by which [these] meditations are differentiated. 133.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, because an option (vikalpa) is determined for all the vidyās since they possess a single fruit. 134.
Since it is understood that this serves the purpose of human endeavor, there is no mandatory rule for the meditation on the *udgītha*.
If [one performs] those rites consisting of sacrifice, I worship that *brāhmaṇa* named Śrīnivāsa. (135)

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, established through the Vedic texts, by the attainment of whose fruit results from the meditation [performed] with the assistance of various respective karmas. 136.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, who is enjoined by the Śruti to be meditated upon as the "most flavorful" (rasatama) in the Udgītha within the ritual action consisting of sacrifice. 137.
I worship that Brāhmaṇa named Śrīnivāsa, by whose narratives concerning Śvetaketu and others at the commencement of the Ṣaḍvidyā and other teachings, those very sciences are glorified. 138.

I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, who does not desire sacrifices and the like among those belonging to the stages of life (āśramas) who are not entitled to perform sacrifices and other such rites.

I worship that heart-essence named Śrīnivāsa, who desires all the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires for those entitled to perform sacrifices, as well as whatever knowledge they seek.

I worship that name Śrīnivāsa, which—though even for those entitled to perform sacrifices, knowledge depends upon tranquility, self-control, and other such qualities—because it is prescribed as a subordinate element (aṅga) [of the sacrifice]. 141.

I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, for even for one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) and possesses extraordinary power, there is a restriction regarding food when it concerns the context of extreme distress.

I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, who is the constituent part of the sacrificial rites and other duties that serve as limbs of His worship, and who is also the limb of the stages of life (āśrama), due to the difference in their application. 143.
Since perfection can be attained even through one's own appropriate acts such as charity and recitation, [the Lord] remains detached;
I worship that heart-pleasing name of Śrīnivāsa, which He employs for His own worship. 144.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, for those who have fallen from their stage of life—such as renunciation (saṃnyāsa)—have no qualification for its meditation. 145.

I worship that Brāhmaṇa named Śrīnivāsa, by whom all knowledges of the *udgītha*—which are auxiliary to the sacrifice and require the assistance of *vidyā*—are to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). 146.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, which is ordained as the mental reflection upon the auspicious refuge, acting as a cooperative cause for meditative concentration and the like. 147.
I worship that name "Śrīnivāsa," which is the manifestation of the greatness ordained for one who is devoted to knowledge and possesses supreme majesty. 148.
Destiny does not yield the fruit of sovereignty such that knowledge arises only at that specific time;
even when duties have been performed, I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa. 149.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, at which time even the most powerful ignorance arises, provided there is no powerful obstacle present. 150.
I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, established by the unanimous voice of the Vedas as that knowledge which must be repeated again and again as the means to liberation. 151.

Although there is a difference in the essential nature of the two—the one to be meditated upon and the meditator, namely the Supreme Being and the individual soul—there is nonetheless an injunction for their identity through the powers [of the Lord], which effects the state of the body being identical with the Self. (152)
Since that which is to be meditated upon as "the Self" has been enjoined by the meditator, I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa who is to be meditated upon as the "Self. 153.
Since name and other such qualities perceived as objects of meditation are not the Self, that which is to be meditated upon as the Self—that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa—I worship. 154.

I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, by whom it was ordained that the meditation on Āditya is appropriate specifically for the *udgītha*—the very limb of the sacrifice that serves as an auxiliary to that meditation. 155.

I worship that name Śrīnivāsa, which is the heart [of all], and whose meditation must be performed even by one who is merely sitting, according to the rule, for the sake of attaining one-pointed concentration. 156.
I worship that heart-essence named Śrīnivāsa, which is to be meditated upon daily by the meditator for as long as life lasts, because it is so ordained in the Vedas. 157.

When, through the power of repeated practice of meditation, the attainment of a form identical to that of the vision is accomplished, there occurs the total destruction of all previously committed sins. (158)
There is no attachment to the sins committed subsequently through negligence;
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa by virtue of the majesty of which [this occurs]. 159.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by whose very knowledge you experience the destruction of past and future merits and demerits, and the non-clinging of new ones at the end of the body. 160.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by which there is the destruction of even those two previously committed [sins] that were not yet active in yielding their fruit. 161.

All the duties of the stages of life (āśramas), even by one who does not desire their fruits and who knows them, must be performed for the sake of knowledge; I worship that Brahman whose name is Śrīnivāsa. 162.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by the experience of which the karmas of a male lay-devotee (upāsaka) that have begun to yield fruit must be exhausted. 163.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, by whose volition all the senses of a living being are joined with the mind at the time of death. 164.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, whose mind is joined with all the senses through volition and is united with the vital breath (prāṇa). 165.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart, which—joined with the mind together with the instruments of action and united with the vital breath by the Person—clings [to the body] through its own volition. 166.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, by whose volition the vital breath, joined with the person and accompanied by the elements, becomes united [with the body]. 167.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, by whose will this departure [from the body] is common to both those devoted to meditation and others. 168.

I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart (hṛdaya) wherein the subtle elements, along with the instruments [the senses], the mind, the vital breath, and the individual soul (jīva), all merge together. 169.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, in which, at the time of death, there occurs the specific conjunction of the gross and subtle living beings. 170.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by whose grace the wise man departs from his own body through the hundred-and-first channel at the crown of the head.
Having followed the rays of the sun, he departs from the body;
that heart which the wise man enters through divine grace—that I worship as the Brahman named Śrīnivāsa. 172.
I worship that heart which bears the name Śrīnivāsa, by the destruction of all karmas even as a lay devotee dies at night, one attains that [state] without delay. (173)
I worship that supreme Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, by practicing whose knowledge one attains that very Brahman even while dying during the southern solstice.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by meditating upon which everyone, through the single path beginning with light (arcis), attains its worlds. 175.

I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, whom the lay devotee (upāsaka), having reached the year on the path beginning with light (arcis) and so forth, subsequently attains as he proceeds toward the wind.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, whom the lay devotee reaches after attaining lightning on the path beginning with light, and then Varuṇa, Indra, and finally Brahman. 177.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by whom the persons beginning with Arcis are appointed to lead those devoted to His worship along the path during their journey across the great distances. 178.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, who, as the host of escorting deities for both the knower of the five fires and the knower of the Veda, leads them across according to his assignment. 179.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by whose attainment this [soul], whose form was concealed by karma, becomes manifest in its true nature. 180.
I worship that which is named Śrīnivāsa, the heart, by virtue of which this person, liberated from the karma of bondage, experiences his own self as a specific attribute. 181.
I worship that Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, by attaining which the individual soul becomes self-luminous through the manifestation of qualities such as freedom from evil (apahatapāpmatva). 182.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, by being intent on serving which one, liberated from mere conceptualization, attains all desired objects.
I worship that heart named Śrīnivāsa, whose divine play it is to experience—having sometimes been embodied and sometimes become bodiless—liberated according to its own will. 184.
Liberated, he attains supreme equality with that which is devoid of any talk of separation; I worship that heart, whose name is Śrīnivāsa. 185.
May this *Adhikaraṇaratnamālā*, strung together by the venerable Śrīdeśikārya,
bring delight and be victorious in the heart of Śrī Śrīnivāsa.
